newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mostly higher.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mostly higher.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended higher across most delivery months Thursday, with the exception of nearby platinum and palladium futures.
Gold and silver prices got some support from this week's surge in platinum group metals prices due to continued disruption of Russian supplies and the brief strike at South Africa's Rustenberg mine.
The dispute between the German government and Bundesbank over revaluing the latter's gold reserves was also supportive because it may make European central bank gold sales less likely, analysts said.

"Gold received some help from the PGMs via the spreads, while silver was up on some EFP buying and cash market borrowing," said Dinsa Mehta, Chase Manhattan managing director for global commodities in New York.

"But the spat between the German government and the Bundesbank, and the problem the Swiss government is also having revaluing its gold reserves, highlights the tortuous path ahead for European governments wanting to mobilize their gold reserves and may actual sales less likely," he said.
COMEX August gold, now the active contract, ended up $1.00 at $348.60 an ounce after edging up to a nine-day high of $349.20. Estimated COMEX gold volume was a high 68,000 lots.

Friday is first notice day for June gold and open interest fell 15,598 lots Wednesday, while August's open interest rose 16,631 lots. Total COMEX gold open interest rose 3,239 lots Wednesday to 162,050 contracts.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted at $345.50/$346.00 against the London Thursday afternoon fix of $343.90.
Thursday, German finance minister Theo Waigel defended his plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves to market value to help Germany meet European Monetary Union (EMU) debt-to-GDP criteria.
But the plan faced a chorus of criticism from the German parliamentary opposition and the media, after the Bundesbank publicly announced its opposition Wednesday.
Bundesbank gold reserves total about 95 million ounces and revaluing them could boost total gold and foreign currency reserves by about 20 billion marks ($11 billion).
"The gold revaluation will boost total reserves, allowing Germany to sell some foreign currency reserves to reduce debt," said Ted Kempf, analyst with CPM Group in New York.
Under EU accounting rules, one off assets sales may be used to the EMU debt-to-GDP criteria, but are not admissable as revenue to reduce the government's budget deficit.
"The bottom line is gold sales by the Bundesbank are still unlikely," Merrill Lynch's New York director of commodities research, Bill O'Neill said.
COMEX July silver ended up 10.8 cents at $4.830 an ounce, after also seeing a nine-day high intraday at $4.845.
NYMEX July platinum ended down 20 cents at $410.30, but not before seeing a new contract high at $420.50 early.
But NYMEX October platinum ended up $2.30 an ounce at $403.80, pushing up the October NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread to a new high for the two contracts at $52.30 an ounce.
In the spot market, platinum was fixed in London Thursday at $417.40, its highest level since February 21, 1996, while lease rates were quoted around 30 percent, after seeing higher levels intraday.
NYMEX June palladium ended down $9.40 an ounce at $193.25, but September palladium ended up $9.00 an ounce at $185.00 and both contracts saw new contract highs intraday.
Friday is first notice day for June palladium.
In the cash market, palladium was fixed at a new all time high at $196.50 in London Thursday, while palladium lease rates remained very high around 50 percent.

"The PGMs market is bedlam," one PGM dealer said. "There is heavy borrowing going on and good demand from the Japanese in the physical market and on TOCOM (Tokyo Commodity Exchange) while the Japanese are still trying to structure some deals with the Russians.
A spokesman for Russian metals export agency, Almaz, said Thursday Russian exports of PGMs were expected to resume late June.
Russian supplies of platinum group metals have been disrupted since last December.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
